# About this app  
The goal of this app is to make the use of environmental DNA (eDNA) accessible to users on the ground working in conservation management. No prior experience with bioinformatics is necessary, and minimal prior data manipulation. All you need to use this app is DNA amplicon sequencing output and a metadata file connecting the sequencing data to your samples. It is meant to distill information into helpful graphics and analyses that can be used for management reports. 

With this, you will get information regarding what species are in your samples, how the community composition and diversity differs between samples, and follow patterns in specific taxa.

This report is a distillation of the analyses ran within the app. If anything is missing, feel free to go back into the app to perform those analyses and then rerun this report.  




This was developed with support from the Marine Conservation Lab at the Smithsonian Environmental Research Center.  


```{r logographic, out.width='25%',fig.align='right', fig.pos='b', include=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("www/MCL_SERC.png")
```

# Dataset overview
This section will go over the characteristics of the dataset that you analyzed. *This is general information that will speak to the quality of the data and how to interpret the results.*    

In addition, this will summarize some basic features of the data, including the distribution of sequences per sample in the total dataset and the one you ultimately analyzed.  

## About the data manipulation choices:   

### Data filtering  

#### 1. Size constraints   
Removing ASVs with only one occurrence can reduce the likelihood of overestimating diversity. Samples with dramatically fewer sequences can also bias analyses.  
  
_Samples with less than `r params$pnsamp` sequences were removed from the dataset._   
_ASVs occurring less than `r params$pntax` times in the dataset were removed._  

#### 2. Normalized data  
Normalizing a dataset is done to make findings comparable across samples with uneven sequencing depth. Relative abundance calculates the proportion of the total for each taxa. Rarefaction will randomly subsample the sequences in each sample to match the number of the smallest sample.  

_Normalization method:_ `r params$norm`  

#### 3. Blanks  
During the process of collecting samples, filtering water, or performing PCR, you likely had 'blanks' for quality control and to track any sources of contamination.   

_The following were selected as your blanks:_  
```{r listblanks}
params$blanks
```
_Were blanks removed?_ `r params$rembl`  

#### 4. Specific sample and taxa choices  
You had the option to specify specific samples to analyze instead of the entire dataset. Similarly, you could have selected specific taxa to include or exclude. 

_Specific samples removed:_ `r params$remsam`

`r if(!is.na(params$unass)) (paste0("You chose to ",params$unass," the following taxa:")) else "You kept all taxa for analysis"`  
```{r listtaxa}
params$remtax
```

# Basic stats    
This section is a sanity check.  
The information we get from this page is useful because it can be used for troubleshooting and can tell us about the quality and reliability of the data we're looking at. Large, dramatic changes here could be the reason why you see differences in what species are showing up or why community composition appears to change. We want to know if the changes are real, biological changes or due to the dataset.  

### Mean, median, etc.    
This is an overview of sequences, ASVs, and how that changes depending on the filtering parameters. You probably don't need to look too far into this, but it will tell you how well your sequences clustered into distinct units/ASVs, how much contamination was found in the blanks (if you defined blanks in the review section), and the spread/evenness of sequences within the dataset.  

#### Of the original dataset:  
```{r ogseqmean}
if (any(is.na(params$numog)==FALSE))  (
  knitr::kable(params$numog,
               digits=2,
               caption="Description of sequencing reads") %>%
    kableExtra::kable_styling(.,
                              bootstrap_options = "bordered",
                              full_width=FALSE,
                              position = "left")
  ) else "Characteristics of your sequencing run were not calculated" 
```

#### Of the subsetted dataset:  
(This could be the same, depending on whether or not you chose to do any dataset manipulations)  

```{r subseqmean}
if (any(is.na(params$numsam)==FALSE)) (
  knitr::kable(params$numsam,
               digits=2,
               caption="Description of the subset you analyzed") %>% 
    kableExtra::kable_styling(params$numsam,
                              bootstrap_options = "bordered",
                              full_width=FALSE,
                              position = "left")
  ) else "Characteristics of the analyzed dataset were not calculated"
```

_Total number of sequences_: `r params$N_seq_total_num_sel`  
_Number of assigned sequences_: `r params$N_seq_assigned_num_sel`  

_Total number of OTUs_: `r params$N_otu_total_num_sel`  
_Number of assigned OTUs_: `r params$N_otu_assigned_num_sel`  


_Number of sequences in blanks_: `r params$N_seq_blanks_num_sel`  
_Number of OTUs in blanks_: `r params$N_otu_blanks_num_sel`

```{r progresstwo}
incProgress(2/11)
Sys.sleep(2)
```

### Sample distribution    
This is a table that shows each of the samples in the dataset you are looking at and how many sequences are in that sample. We want to know if one sample has way more (or less) sequences than the rest of the dataset - unbalanced data makes it difficult to see real patterns.  

Remember that if data were normalized this number might look unusual.  
_Normalization method:_ `r params$norm`  
```{r seqspersample}
if (any(is.na(params$samsum)==FALSE)) (
  knitr::kable(params$samsum,
               digits=2,
               caption="Sequence distribution") %>% 
    kableExtra::kable_styling(params$samsum,
                              bootstrap_options = "bordered",
                              full_width=FALSE,
                              position = "left")
  ) else "Sequence distribution not calculated"
```

```{r progressthree}
incProgress(3/11)
Sys.sleep(2)
```

### Sequence distribution   
In this plot, we are looking at the number of sequences in each sample. 

This tool is a useful gut check to get a high-level overview of the entire dataset. Do any samples have significantly more or less sequences than another? That is normally a signal that some kind of normalization will be needed prior to performing any analyses or that there should have been a higher cutoff for sample number.  
```{r seqdist} 
p_bar <- plot_bar(params$ps,
                   title="Number of sequences per sample") 

 #+ geom_line(aes(y=100000,color="green")) #add horizontal line at 100,000 to show goal minimum sequencing depth 

(p_bar)
```

```{r progressfour}
incProgress(4/11)
Sys.sleep(2)
```

## Taxonomy  

### Unique taxa  
This is a table showing how many unique taxonomic groups can be found at each rank. This is a useful way to look at the general diversity of your data, and ask if it matches up with what you'd expect from the marker you chose. Do you expect a variety of phyla? Or were you using specifically targetted primers?  
```{r}
if (any(is.na(params$ntaxa)==FALSE)) (
  knitr::kable(params$ntaxa,
               caption="Overview of the diversity of taxa found in your dataset") %>% 
    kableExtra::kable_styling(params$ntaxa,
                              bootstrap_options = "bordered",
                              full_width=FALSE,
                              position = "left")
) else "Taxonomic diversity was not summarized"
```

```{r}
incProgress(5/11)
Sys.sleep(2)
```
